transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Amy Held.
The FAA is examining Friday's ground stop that is still disrupting flights more than
7,000 so far today.
NPR's Ava Berger reports Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy says it started with the contractors'
work on old copper wires.
NPR reached out for comment from L3 Harris.
In a public statement, the company said that it has been working with the FAA to convert
those old wires to a fiber-optic system.
And it says it has completed more than 70 percent of those conversions.
L3 Harris said it is supporting the FAA in their investigation.
In a video on the company's website, L3 Harris touts the work the company is doing to update
the FAA's communication systems.
The brand-new air traffic control system will enhance safety, reduce delays and pave the
way for new technologies like flying taxis and drones.
The website also says its FAA telecom infrastructure supports 45,000 daily flights.
Ava Berger, NPR News, Washington.
Investors will be watching NVIDIA's quarterly earnings due out this week following the ouster
of the company's scandal-ridden CEO, The New York Times reports President Trump was told
about Jensen Huang's affair with a suspected Chinese spy, but did not act.
Ricky Mulvey with the indicator from Planet Money reports Alice Huang's then-company
Megaspeed had business dealings with NVIDIA.
Investigators at the Commerce Department raised some flags about this company a couple of
years ago.
They thought it was unusual that Megaspeed had NVIDIA chips just packed in boxes at its
data center in Malaysia, sort of like leaving Amazon packages in your entrance way except
with highly coveted AI chips.
In a statement provided to NPR, Megaspeed says it conducts lawful and legitimate business
and that Alice Huang left the company last year.
Now, Culper Research, a short seller or someone who bets against companies, noted their uncomfortably
close relationship back in May.
So in other words, there was some smoke long before this fire.
Russian attacks killed four people and injured 69 others across Ukraine over the past day,
Ukrainian authorities say.
NPR's Eleanor Beardsley reports.
"Air raid sirens went off throughout Sunday in Kiev and other cities across the country.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia had launched more than 2,300 attack
drones, 1,590 glide bombs, and 15 missiles of various types against Ukraine over the
past week.
He said continued restrictions on the speed of Star Shield, the militarized version of
Starlink, are preventing Ukrainian interceptor drones from taking down jet-powered Shahad
drones.
Russian forces are targeting energy substations with the Shahad drones.
Zelensky said many of the strikes get through precisely because speed restrictions remain
in place."
Eleanor Beardsley, NPR News, Kiev.
This is NPR News.
NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft is about to achieve a major long-distance milestone.
I'm here as John Stoleness reports.
It's already flown farther from Earth than any man-made spacecraft ever, but at just
after 5 a.m. Eastern time on Wednesday, Voyager 1 will have traveled one light day away from
Earth.
That's about 16 billion miles, or the distance light travels in 24 hours.
Voyager 1 launched with its twin, Voyager 2, in 1977, and traveling at almost 38,000
miles an hour, discovered new moons and rings around both Jupiter and Saturn.
Voyager 2 took a different route to deep space in order to visit Uranus in Neptune.
It is scheduled to reach the light-day milestone nine years from now.
John Stoleness, NPR News.
Starship's 22-hour round trip to orbit and back this weekend marks a breakthrough for
SpaceX.
The 15th test flight is the first successful landing of a rocket's upper stage and gets
SpaceX closer to its goal of one day making Starship a rapidly reusable rocket.
It didn't quite land its hope for double-catch.
The booster exploded and crashed into the sea.
A Georgia O'Keefe painting buried behind coats and boxes has come to light.
A Manhattan woman kept the depiction of a New Mexico landscape in her apartment closet
for decades.
She died recently in her 90s, and now the artwork is going up for auction Tuesday, estimated
to bring in millions.
O'Keefe is known for her 20th century abstract paintings of flowers and scenes of the Southwest,
which she called home.
This is NPR News.

topics.text: FAA investigating Friday ground stop disrupting over 7,000 flights, linked to L3Harris copper wire work
NVIDIA faces investor scrutiny after CEO ouster, with reports Trump was told of Jensen Huang's affair with suspected Chinese spy
Ukraine reports four killed and 69 injured in Russian attacks over the past day, per Eleanor Beardsley
NASA's Voyager 1 nears one light day from Earth, a long-distance milestone
SpaceX Starship completes 15th test flight with first successful upper-stage landing, booster lost at sea
Georgia O'Keeffe painting found hidden in Manhattan woman's closet to be auctioned Tuesday, estimated worth millions
